anchor: They that have power to hurt
title: They that have power to hurt
short: Those who could do harm but choose not to; whether this praises self-control or exposes cold, manipulative restraint is the poem's central crux.
body: The octave seems to praise people of self-possession who do not use their power to wound. But 'power to hurt' may include sexual power, the power to break hearts, and the cold, unmoved figure of ll. 3-4 sounds less admirable than calculating. Empson's famous chapter reads the sonnet as an ironic network of praise and blame directed at someone like the young man of the surrounding sonnets (Sonnet 93 speaks of a beautiful but possibly false face). Booth argues the syntax never lets the reader settle. Older critics such as Tyler took the praise more simply, while noting Angelo in Measure for Measure as the corrupt version of such a character.

title: do not do the thing they most do show
short: Who do not carry out what their appearance most suggests or seems to threaten, whether harm or desire.
body: The line hangs on the repeated verb 'do' (do not do / most do show). It may mean they do not do the hurt they show they could do, or they do not act on the passion their beauty seems to promise. Either way the line separates outward show from deed, a theme of Sonnet 93 too. Booth notes the deliberately slippery syntax; Duncan-Jones relates it to the young man's beauty, which invites a love he does not return.

title: moving others, are themselves as stone
short: They move others to feeling while staying unmoved, cold and slow to temptation, like stone.
body: The paradox of the 'unmoved mover' sits in 'moving others ... Unmoved'. Stone is an image of hardness and coldness (a Petrarchan commonplace for the cruel beloved), and Shakespeare stresses the coldness with 'Unmoved, cold'. 'To temptation slow' could be virtue (chastity, Stoic constancy) or mere lack of feeling. Tyler compares Hamlet's praise of Horatio, who is 'not a pipe for Fortune's finger'. Empson and later readers hear coldness, not virtue, in the accumulated adjectives.

anchor: They rightly do inherit heaven's graces
title: inherit heaven's graces
short: Such people rightly receive heaven's gifts, as heirs; biblical language of inheritance and grace.
body: 'Inherit' recalls the Beatitudes ('the meek ... shall inherit the earth', Matthew 5:5) and Matthew 25:34 ('inherit the kingdom prepared for you'). 'Heaven's graces' are both spiritual grace and the physical graces (beauty) given by heaven. 'Rightly' means justly, deservedly, but also by right of inheritance. Booth notes that the economic and religious senses mix here, leading to 'husband' and 'stewards'.

title: husband ... from expense
short: They manage and save nature's gifts, guarding them against being spent or wasted.
body: 'Husband' as a verb means to manage thriftily, to save (OED), from the sense of a householder who manages an estate. 'Expense' means spending, waste. They do not squander their beauty or energy, which Tyler glosses as not spending themselves in passionate outbursts. Readers of the procreation sonnets (1-17) will recall the opposite charge, that the young man wastes himself by not having children; Booth and Duncan-Jones note the tension. 'Expense' returns, in a sexual sense, in Sonnet 129.

anchor: lords and owners of their faces
title: lords and owners of their faces
short: They have full control of their own faces and expressions; they own their beauty outright.
body: To be 'lord and owner' is to have full legal possession. They govern their own faces, showing no involuntary emotion (Tyler: not giving ready expression to feeling), and they possess their beauty absolutely rather than holding it in trust. The phrase looks back to Sonnet 93, where the friend's face may hide falseness. Vendler and Booth note the property language that runs from 'inherit' through 'husband' to 'owners' and 'stewards'.

anchor: Others, but stewards of their excellence
title: stewards of their excellence
short: Everyone else is only a steward, a manager holding goods for a master; the image recalls the biblical parables of stewards and talents.
body: A steward manages property for an owner and must account for it. The line is ambiguous: 'their excellence' may be the excellence of these self-possessed people, served by others; or other people's own excellence, which they merely hold on loan. The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30) and the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16:1-8) lie behind the language; 1 Peter 4:10 calls Christians 'good stewards of the manifold grace of God'. Empson notes the irony that the parable of the talents condemns the servant who hoards rather than uses his gift, which turns the octave's praise of 'husbanding' against itself.

title: The summer's flower
short: The sestet shifts to a parable: a summer flower gives sweetness to the season even though it lives and dies only for itself.
body: The turn at l. 9 abandons the economic language for an image from nature. The flower is sweet to the summer even if it 'only' lives and dies for itself, in solitude. The lines may praise self-contained beauty or hint at its sterility, recalling the self-loving youth of the procreation sonnets (cf. Sonnet 54, also on flowers and scent). Tyler's headnote says the flower is still sweet though its sweetness is wasted on the desert air (the phrase is Gray's, from his Elegy). Vendler treats the sestet as a revision of the octave's ideal.

title: base infection
short: If that flower becomes infected by some low corruption (disease, canker, or moral fault).
body: 'Base' means low, ignoble, and its repetition in 'basest weed' (l. 12) ties the corruption to the lowest of plants. 'Infection' suggests a canker or blight in the flower, and morally, contamination by vice. Many readers connect the line with the canker-worm imagery elsewhere in the sequence (Sonnets 35, 70, 95) and with venereal infection, though that reading is not certain. Booth discusses the range of sense.

title: outbraves his dignity
short: The lowest weed surpasses the flower's worth; 'outbrave' = outshine, defy, exceed in finery.
body: 'Brave' in Elizabethan English often means splendid, finely dressed; to 'outbrave' is to outdo in splendour or to defy (OED). The weed, despised but uncorrupted, now looks finer than the infected flower. 'His dignity' means its rank or worth ('his' as the old neuter possessive). The line sets up the proverbial couplet. The reversal of high and low (flower beneath weed) is the sestet's key move, since rank and beauty count for nothing once corruption sets in.

title: sweetest things turn sourest
short: The best things become the worst when corrupted by what they do; a version of the proverb 'corruptio optimi pessima'.
body: The Latin proverb 'the corruption of the best is the worst' was widely known in the period, and editors gloss the line as proverbial. 'By their deeds' brings back the distinction between showing and doing in l. 2: what people do, not what they show, determines their worth. The alliteration and antithesis (sweetest / sourest) give the couplet the force of a maxim.

title: Lilies that fester (Edward III)
short: Rotting lilies smell worse than weeds; the identical line occurs in the play Edward III (printed 1596), now often attributed partly to Shakespeare.
body: The line appears in Edward III, Act 2 (scene numbering varies), in the Earl of Warwick's speech on the corruption of great persons, in a scene many scholars assign to Shakespeare. Which came first is disputed: the play was printed in 1596, but the sonnet may have been written earlier or later. Lilies are emblems of purity, so their festering (rotting, putrefying) makes the stench of corruption worse by contrast. Tyler takes the lilies as colourless, passionless natures, as against the blushing rose. The poem ends on a moral smell, answering the 'sweet' flower of l. 9.
